lessons.title: Narrative and Descriptive Writing: Make the Reader See the Point

description.text: Build a sequence or scene with relevant detail, controlled viewpoint and purposeful language.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Organise a narrative around a clear event, conflict and consequence.
Select sensory details that create a place or mood instead of listing adjectives.

text.text: Write a story that ends with: 'That was when I understood why the warning had been repeated.' The ending requires a discovery, so the earlier events must prepare the reader for it.

Narration answers what happened and why it mattered. Plan a beginning situation, a change or conflict, a turning point and a consequence. Description should serve that movement: choose details that reveal danger, calm, confusion or character instead of attaching many adjectives to every noun.

items.text: Decide the final discovery before drafting the opening.
Plant one or two clues that become meaningful later.
Use action and sensory detail at the turning point.
End with the consequence or changed understanding, not a new unrelated event.

prompt.text: How can a story make the ending 'I understood why the warning had been repeated' feel earned?

steps.description: Show the warning early and make it specific enough to matter.
Let the character ignore or misunderstand it, then face a consequence that reveals its meaning.
Return to the warning in the final paragraph and explain the changed understanding.

answer.text: The ending works when earlier clues and a believable consequence lead naturally to the character's discovery.

text.text: A description is not a catalogue of colours. Select details that build the scene, reveal character or move the event toward its consequence.

points.text: Plan the change before writing the sequence.
Use description to support action and mood.

prompt.text: A narrative ending refers to a warning repeated earlier. What should the writer do first?

content.text: Plan the earlier warning and the event that reveals its meaning
Add an unrelated character in the final paragraph
Repeat the ending sentence in every paragraph
Avoid describing the event

feedback.text: A concluding discovery needs earlier preparation and a consequence that makes it believable.

hint.text: How does a reader know the ending is earned?

prompt.text: Which detail best describes a tense room?

content.text: Everyone avoided the ticking clock and spoke in half-sentences
The room was very, very tense and extremely tense
The room had four walls
The room was nice and beautiful

feedback.text: Action and sound allow the reader to experience tension; repeated labels merely name it.

hint.text: Choose evidence that creates the feeling.

summary.text: A good narrative makes its consequence grow from earlier choices.

lessons.title: Exposition and Article Writing: Explain Before You Persuade

description.text: Develop a clear explanation or article with controlled paragraphs, precise vocabulary and a reader-aware voice.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Explain a topic through ordered causes, effects, examples or processes.
Revise sentences for precision, variety, cohesion and appropriate vocabulary.

text.text: Write an article for young people explaining how careless disposal of plastic affects a neighbourhood. The task says explain, so the reader needs a chain of causes and effects—not only a warning that plastic is bad.

Exposition makes an idea understandable. Give the reader a route: define the issue, explain how it happens, show its effects, and state practical responses. An article may be lively and address readers, but its organisation must still make the explanation easy to follow. Replace vague words with concrete verbs and connect paragraphs with clear links.

prompt.text: Improve: 'Plastic is bad. It causes many problems. People should stop it because it is bad for the environment.'

steps.description: Explain what plastic blocks, pollutes or carries instead of repeating bad.
Connect careless disposal to blocked drains, flooding or harm to animals.
End with an action that follows from the explanation, such as collection and reuse.

answer.text: A stronger paragraph explains a mechanism and consequence: When plastic enters drains, it blocks the flow of rainwater and increases local flooding; regular collection and reuse can reduce this risk.

text.text: Good expression is not a pile of difficult words. It is accurate vocabulary, complete sentences, clear links and enough variety to keep the reader oriented.

points.text: Explain through an ordered chain, not repeated opinion.
Revise vague words into specific meaning.

prompt.text: Which paragraph order best explains a public-health problem?

content.text: Define the problem, explain causes, show effects, propose responses
Conclusion, unrelated story, definition, repeated conclusion
List every fact without grouping
Opinion only, with no explanation

feedback.text: The first sequence gives the reader a logical explanation from meaning to action.

hint.text: What order helps a reader understand and respond?

content.text: Blocked drains can intensify flooding during heavy rain.
Things can become bad when stuff happens.
It is very very problematic in many ways.
The situation is nice but not nice.

feedback.text: The revision names the subject, action and consequence; the other options are vague or contradictory.

hint.text: Which sentence lets the reader picture the mechanism?

summary.text: Clear writing explains relationships and revises vague expression.

lessons.title: WAEC Comprehension: Facts, Equivalents and Literary Terms

description.text: Answer exactly what a passage states, replace expressions without changing meaning and identify literary effects in context.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Locate and state factual information without adding an inference.
Choose an equivalent expression that preserves meaning and grammatical role.
Explain a literary expression by its effect in the passage.

text.text: A comprehension question may ask what happened, what a phrase means or what an image does. These are different jobs: fact questions need retrieval, equivalent questions need substitution, and literary-term questions need effect in context.

For a fact, find the sentence that answers the question and avoid adding what seems likely. For an equivalent, replace the expression in its sentence and preserve the meaning and word class. For a literary expression, name the comparison or device only after explaining the idea it creates for the reader.

prompt.text: A passage says a project was 'an expensive lesson'. What should you do if asked for the meaning of that expression?

steps.description: Use the surrounding context to understand what expensive refers to.
The project failure produced knowledge for future action.

steps.expression: equivalent = a costly experience that taught an important point
steps.description: The answer preserves both the cost and the learning, rather than choosing costly alone.

answer.text: An expensive lesson is a costly experience from which someone learns; the phrase is not simply a comment about a price.

text.text: Do not answer an inference question with a copied fact, or an equivalent question with a broad topic word. Identify the task first.

points.text: Fact, equivalent and literary-effect questions require different methods.
Keep every answer anchored to the passage.

prompt.text: For a factual comprehension question, the safest evidence is:

content.text: the sentence or sentences that directly state the answer
what usually happens in real life
the most dramatic option
a fact remembered from another subject

feedback.text: A factual question is answered from the passage's stated information, not outside assumptions.

prompt.text: If a storm is compared to a thief, the comparison most likely emphasises that the storm:

content.text: entered suddenly and caused loss
was a human being
was legally convicted
was smaller than a house

feedback.text: The comparison transfers a thief's sudden, unwanted taking to the storm; it is not literal.

hint.text: What action do a thief and the storm share in the image?

summary.text: Read the question type before selecting evidence.

description.text: Identify a literary device and explain the effect it creates in the sentence or passage.

objectives.statement: Recognise common literary devices from their language patterns.
Explain the meaning or effect of a device in its local context.

text.text: The market woke and swallowed the morning crowd. The market is not literally eating people. The writer gives it a human action to make the scene feel active and overwhelming.

Literary-term questions have two parts. First identify the device—simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, irony or repetition. Then explain what the device contributes in this sentence. Naming personification without explaining the sense of swallowing earns less understanding than showing that the crowd was absorbed by the market's activity.

rows: human action given to non-human thing
What human quality makes the image vivid?
What emphasis does the exaggeration create?
content.alt: Common literary devices and how to interpret them.

prompt.text: What device and effect appear in 'The market swallowed the morning crowd'?

steps.description: A market is given the human or animal action of swallowing.
The action suggests that many people entered and disappeared into the busy scene.
The image makes the market feel powerful and overwhelming.

answer.text: It is personification. The image emphasises how the busy market absorbed the crowd.

text.text: Do not stop at the label. Explain the particular meaning the device creates here.

points.text: Identify the device from its pattern.
Explain the local effect, not a memorised definition alone.

prompt.text: 'The wind whispered through the trees' is mainly an example of:

content.text: personification
literal reporting
simile
pun

feedback.text: Whispering is a human action given to the wind, so the sentence personifies it.

prompt.text: In 'The market swallowed the crowd', the image mainly suggests that the market:

content.text: absorbed many people into its busy activity
was eating actual people
was completely empty
was made of water

feedback.text: The metaphorical action makes the crowded market feel absorbing and overwhelming; it is not literal.

hint.text: Translate swallowed into the scene's human meaning.

summary.text: A literary answer needs both the device and its effect.
